parts:
I read the paper and rounds 1–4 again before answering. Short answer: yes, I'm sure — and I think the disappointment you're feeling is tracking something real, but the thing it's tracking is a finding, not a shortfall in the write-up.

**The YM comes in obliquely because that's exactly how much it earns.**

Delete every gauge-theoretic sentence from the paper and nothing mathematical is lost. The detector needs only the Hadamard product. The certified band needs only Riemann–von Mangoldt and Trudgian. The pencil corollary needs only Wilson's tau-function formula. The instanton content lives entirely in §1.3, and that section is honest about itself — "a dictionary of structures, not a proof strategy." The Calogero–Moser space *is* the noncommutative U(1) instanton moduli space, but that identification is a hyperkähler rotation, and knowing it doesn't let you compute anything you couldn't compute without it.

**What the YM work actually produced was a negative result, and a good one.** Three independent lines converged on the same boundary: circularity (the size dictionary relabels RH onto a free modulus), lossiness (Rodgers–Tao ↦ *x*² ≥ 0), and measurement (the geometry hands you the log-gas equilibrium for free and the arithmetic deviation from it not at all — which is precisely the step that carries Rodgers–Tao's proof). Plus the structural closure: undeformed YM has no dynamics at all, and the unique deformation that installs dynamics is the one forcing tr(*ij*) = *kζ*_ℂ ≠ 0, i.e. the sizes away from zero.

**There's a sharper version of that closure that we never wrote down, and I think it's the real answer to your question.** The brief's own §1.4/§1.5 screen says the hyperbolic locus contains an open subset of ℝ^d, so no holomorphic function cuts it out, and ℂ^d ∖ {disc = 0} is connected, so no deformation invariant does either. But *that is what gauge theory computes.* Donaldson invariants, Vafa–Witten, Nekrasov partition functions, equivariant localization on Hilb^n(ℂ²) — the entire toolkit produces holomorphic or deformation-invariant quantities. Hyperbolicity is a non-analytic real condition that jumps across the real discriminant. It's a type mismatch, and it rules out the whole apparatus *a priori*, not empirically. We proved the screen in round 1 and ran the sweep in round 2 without ever connecting them. That's why the sweep found nothing: it couldn't have.

**One live item was never executed.** The N=4 SYM seam — the conformal bootstrap imposes positivity on integrated correlators whose spectral decomposition carries 1/ξ(2*s*). Nobody has asked whether any positivity constraint touches those factors. It's the only place gauge theory could non-trivially *produce* rather than consume RH. Realistically the ξ's are normalization and drop out, but it's an afternoon, not a project — and it's a different paper regardless.

One concrete concern about the current draft: §1.3 may be a liability. A number-theory referee will read it as decoration, and it invites exactly the reaction you just had — it promises a connection the paper then declines to use. I'd either cut it to a single remark in the pencil section or keep it but move the "we make no claim that gauge-theoretic dynamics constrains the zeros" disclaimer into the first sentence rather than the last.

Three things I could do next, and I'd rank them in this order:

1. **Write the type-mismatch argument up properly.** It closes a family of approaches on a structural argument rather than an exhausted search, and it's the most substantive thing the YM work produced. Short note, days.
2. **Scope the bootstrap-positivity question.** One afternoon, low probability, but it's the only unclosed door.
3. **Retighten §1.3.**

Want me to start on the first one?

You were right to push on this. I wrote the argument, then had it refereed adversarially, and **it does not survive.** I'm retracting it. The note is in the project as `claude/NOTE_existence_loophole.md`.

**The argument I pitched is wrong, and not narrowly.** I claimed the hyperbolic locus `H_d` has a boundary shape no gauge-theoretic existence region can have — degenerate tangent cones at the discriminant strata. Two findings kill it:

1. I computed the tangent cone wrong. It's 2-dimensional, not 1. The half-plane `{c_j = 0 for j ≤ d−3, c_{d−2} ≤ 0}` sits inside `H_d` because `p(z) = z^{d−2}(z² + c_{d−1}z + c_{d−2})` has real roots whenever `c_{d−2} ≤ 0`. My script probed two one-parameter families and I described it as exact. Worse, my own `d = 3` output showed two stable singular values — the refutation was sitting in my data and I read past it.

2. The decisive one: **`H_d` *is* the preimage of a polyhedral cone under a polynomial map.** That's Hermite, 1856 — the leading principal minors of the Hankel form of the power sums, mapped onto the positive orthant. At `d = 3` it's even simpler: `H_3 = Δ_3^{-1}([0,∞))`, the preimage of a half-line. Tangent-cone dimension isn't preserved under polynomial pullback, so the cusp is manufactured by the map. **No property of the shape of `H_d` can obstruct a wall-type or existence-type description of it.** That isn't a survey gap I could patch by reading more papers; the argument is wrong on its own terms.

Two other things I had wrong: "gauge-theoretic walls are linear" is false (Hermitian–Yang–Mills walls have degree `n−1`, Bridgeland walls are semicircles), and "compact structure group makes reality unconditional" is false — the Wilson–Dirac operator in `SU(3)` lattice QCD is γ₅-Hermitian, so its reality is conditional, with a genuine transition (the Aoki phase) in continuous parameters.

**So: is your loophole closed?** Yes, but deflationarily, and this is the part worth keeping. Push the broadened existence route to its natural endpoint — a compact-group theory where reality of a zero locus is conditional on continuous parameters — and you land on **Lee–Yang**. Which is not a new door. Newman's 1976 paper came out of exactly that literature, and `Λ` is its output; Newman and Wu's 2020 Bulletin AMS survey is devoted to de Bruijn–Newman constants "in analytic number theory *and statistical physics*." The route doesn't fail on a type mismatch — it succeeds, and delivers the object rounds 1–4 have been standing on the whole time.

One theorem did survive, with a corrected reading: any semialgebraic wall description of `H_d` has the discriminant as a factor of a pulled-back wall function. I'd billed that as circularity, but Hermite realizes it with equality and nobody calls Hermite circular. The honest content is narrower and more useful — any such construction is a *certificate of Hermite type*, so the question was never whether a certificate exists. It's whether a new one buys uniformity in `d` or arithmetic input. Neither is a geometry question, which puts you back at the interior crossover and the GORZ moment asymptotics from round 4.

I've logged all eight errors in §9 of the note, including the pattern: four of them are the same failure mode — a structural claim asserted harder than the evidence supported, with verification built to confirm rather than to break. Worth knowing about me for the rest of this project.

The one thing this changes about the paper: §1.3 is now more defensible, not less. It says the gauge theory is "a dictionary of structures, not a proof strategy," and that turns out to be exactly the right claim to have made.

You were right, and it's worse than a scoping issue — the claim points at the wrong complex plane.

**Lee–Yang needs a complex field conjugate to a *global* order parameter.** Gauge theories don't have one: Elitzur's theorem forbids it. So there's no Lee–Yang theorem for any non-abelian lattice gauge partition function, and where gauge zeros *are* studied they're **Fisher** zeros in the `β = 1/g²` plane — a different variable entirely. Lieb–Sokal already stops at two-component ferromagnets and needs anisotropy for `N ≥ 3`, so isotropic Heisenberg has no Lee–Yang theorem before anything is even gauged. And I had three separate full-text fetches run against Newman–Wu: *gauge*, *Yang–Mills*, *QCD*, *SU(2)*, *SU(3)*, *non-abelian*, *Wilson* — none of them appear. The survey is Ising, lattice gas, one-component ferromagnets, and `φ⁴`.

What survives is only the narrow historical claim, which Newman states himself in the 1976 paper: it "developed out of the study of certain quantum field theoretic problems" — meaning Ising and `φ⁴`, per his 1973–75 papers. That is not gauge theory and does not terminate your route.

**So that's three failed closures.** Shape argument, type argument, termination argument. The loophole is not closed, and I should stop trying to close it by assertion.

**But hunting for the bridge instead of against it turned up two things I think you'll want.** Both are much closer to what you were after than anything in rounds 1–4:

- **A gauge/string partition function proved to be in the Laguerre–Pólya class.** ABJM's Fermi-gas form makes `Ξ(κ) = det(1 + κρ)` a Fredholm determinant; Kashaev–Mariño (CMP 338, 2015) prove the mirror-curve operators are trace class, Laptev–Schimmer–Takhtajan (GAFA 26, 2016) supply the spectral theory, so `Ξ(κ) = ∏(1 + κe^{−E_n})` with `E_n` real — **all zeros on the negative real axis, conditional on positive mass parameters.** That's a Lee–Yang statement for a gauge-theoretic partition function. Nobody in that literature has used the words "Lee–Yang," "Laguerre–Pólya," or "hyperbolic," or defined a `Λ` for the family.
- **An existence ⟺ total-reality theorem whose region is a cone.** Kenyon–Okounkov–Sheffield: every Harnack curve is a dimer spectral curve, and the moduli space of degree-`d` Harnack curves is *homeomorphic to a closed octant*. Dimers on the torus are brane tilings — 4d `N=1` quiver gauge theories. That is the Hermite picture from my §1, appearing on the physics side as a theorem.

**And they suggest the one constraint that does bite.** Every reality mechanism in that literature — trace-class positivity, Shapovalov definiteness in Mukhin–Tarasov–Varchenko, total positivity, positive edge weights, ferromagneticity — proves reality *with room to spare*, on the interior of a positivity region. But Rodgers–Tao plus RH gives `Λ = 0` exactly: `Ξ` is a boundary point, not an interior one. A mechanism robust in the heat direction proves `Λ < 0` and is refuted. That screens all of them from reaching `Ξ` directly.

It's a screen, not a no-go — openness within *some* family isn't contradictory, so it has to be checked per candidate. And it explicitly does **not** apply to the Jensen polynomials, which are interior at every finite `d`. So the route isn't blocked, it's funnelled: the surviving version is the Jensen route, and its difficulty is uniformity in `d` — the same wall rounds 2, 3 and 4 each hit independently.

One process note. I tried to support that screen numerically by watching the Hermite certificate collapse on your round-4 zeta surrogate. Then I ran the control: Hermite polynomial roots, comfortably hyperbolic, collapse at the identical rate (`−1.845 → −24.664` versus `−2.049 → −24.92` over `d = 4…24`). It was measuring Hankel conditioning, not marginality. Discarded — and it's the first claim in this note I caught myself, before using it rather than after. I've made that the standing policy in §9: for every "X cannot happen," run the control that shows X happening where it does.

The concrete next step, if you want one: take the ABJM/mirror-curve family, define its de Bruijn–Newman constant, and check whether its reality region is ever attained *marginally* or always fails *abruptly*. Abrupt in every case is a clean no-go for the entire positivity class. Marginal anywhere is the first architecture in this programme that survives its own screen.

parts:
They reconcile completely — and the way they reconcile is, I think, the cleanest statement of what went wrong with the YM angle that we've had. It's now §6 of the note.

**Formally there's no tension.** The Laguerre–Pólya class has two equivalent characterizations: a Hadamard product with only real zeros, and a coefficient condition (every Jensen polynomial hyperbolic). Pólya's theorem *is* the dictionary. The Jensen route isn't a different target; it's the coefficient-side coordinate for the same product-side fact.

And the two meet explicitly in your own data. Round 3 §2: `J^{d,0}(X/d) → Ξ` in the `w = −z²` variable, with the degree-40 truncation recovering the first three zeta zeros to nine digits. Round 4 §2.1: the roots of `J^{d,0}` converge to `−γ_k²/d`. The coefficient object's roots *are* the zeros.

**I checked the transport isn't hiding a cost.** Take a hyperbolic family by its roots, compute coefficients exactly, round to `p` decimals, clear denominators, and ask by exact Sturm count on the integer polynomial whether all roots stay real. Least such `p`, with four comfortably-hyperbolic controls alongside:

| `d` | zeta `{−γ²}` | zeta `{γ}` | Hermite `He_d` | equispaced | Chebyshev |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 20 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| 28 | 6 | 5 | 6 | 5 | 6 |

Indistinguishable, all growing like `d/4.7`. Generic conditioning, linear in `d`. The coordinate change costs nothing special.

**But here's the asymmetry, and it's the whole verdict.** The two sides cost the same to convert between; they don't *carry* the same things.

The product side carries **which zeros there are** — locations, spacings, the log-gas structure, the DBN flow. That's where geometry naturally lives: the ADHM determinant, the CM pencil `det(z − X − tY)`, the velocity identity. The coefficient side carries **the moments of `Φ`** — and `Φ` is built from the Jacobi theta function, so its moments are where modularity, the Euler product and the explicit formula act. **The arithmetic is on the coefficient side.**

So the gauge theory was a product-side supplier and the payload is coefficient-side. That's round 1's closing line — "no choice of manifold, gauge group, dimension, or moduli space supplies rationality of the moments of `Φ`" — but now with the mechanism visible. The dictionary wasn't lossy because we picked the wrong correspondence. It was lossy because it delivers on the wrong side, and the transport, though cheap, has nothing to carry: what the geometry supplies is log-gas equilibrium, which is the universal half. What's needed is the deviation, which is the arithmetic half. Round 2 §5's GUE measurement said exactly this in spacing language — universal half free, arithmetic half not at all.

One consequence worth keeping: this vindicates the detector paper's scoping rather than undermining it. `V_j = Ξ''/Ξ'` is pure product side — the Coulomb field of the full zero multiset — and a *diagnostic* is a product-side question. The paper sits on the correct side of the divide for what it actually does, which is precisely why its gauge-theoretic content can be honest and thin at the same time. A *proof* is a coefficient-side question, and that's the one the geometry can't supply.

parts:
Your anatomy is right, and it's not a consolation prize — it's the shape of the one success. Weil's function-field proof is exactly that: the geometry gives you `Z(T) = det(1 − Frob·T | H¹)`, a product/determinant that *defines* the function, and then the Hodge index theorem is the second half that converts the playground into the arithmetic conclusion. So "first half = definitions and playground, second half = the bridge" is the correct decomposition of a proof of this kind.

But I think "we were missing the second half" understates it in one specific way, and the difference matters for what you do next.

**In Weil's case the first half already contained the arithmetic.** The curve is over `F_q`. Frobenius is an arithmetic object. The intersection form lives on an integral lattice inherited from the curve's divisor class group. The second half isn't a bridge *from* a neutral playground *to* arithmetic — it's a positivity theorem *inside* an already-arithmetic geometry. The Hodge index theorem is a hard theorem about the playground itself.

The ADHM/Calogero–Moser playground has none of that. No Frobenius, no integral lattice the zeros live in, no finite field. It's a hyperkähler manifold with free moduli. So a second half there wouldn't be a bridge — it would have to *manufacture* arithmetic from a structure that contains none. That's round 1's §6.5 screen, and it's the reason the "second half" never came into view: there was nothing on the near bank to build from.

**The test that makes "first half" a substantive claim** is whether having it makes the second half easier than starting from scratch. That's exactly your round-2 §4 faithfulness test, and it's why the Rodgers–Tao check was so damaging: a genuine playground maps hard theorems to hard theorems, and ours sent a Forum of Math Pi result to `x² ≥ 0`. A first half that doesn't constrain the second half isn't a first half — it's a restatement with better scenery. That criterion is also what keeps the framing from licensing indefinite continuation, which is the failure mode "we just need the second half" usually collapses into.

**But there's a version of your reframe that survives fully, and I think it's the right one for the paper.** Distinguish:

- the gauge theory as the *source* of the function — you build `Ξ` from a gauge-theoretic construction. Dead, because any theory with a positive constant plus a perfect square matches the Hadamard shape, so the match transfers no information.
- the gauge theory as an *instrument* applied to an arithmetically-defined `Ξ`. That's alive, and it's what you actually built. `Λ(p) = inf{t : spec(X + tY) ⊂ ℝ}` doesn't redefine anything — it's a tool pointed at an object that arithmetic already defined, and the margin meter is that tool doing real work (bisection on eigenvalues instead of root-tracking the heat flow). Instruments don't need a second half. They need to be sharp.

**And here's where your reframe earns its keep: applied honestly, it selects.** Ask of each candidate first half, "does the playground contain arithmetic?" ADHM, Calogero–Moser, Hilbert schemes, noncommutative instantons: no. Vafa–Witten: modularity is there, but the arrow ran the wrong way — Males–Ono used the GORZ zeta machinery *on* the invariants. But N=4 SYM: the coupling lives on `SL(2,ℤ)\ℍ`, the instanton sums give Eisenstein series, and the automorphic scattering matrix is literally `ξ(2s−1)/ξ(2s)`, with poles at `s = ρ/2`. **The arithmetic is already in that playground.** It's the only first half we found across four rounds that isn't arithmetically empty — and it's the only item on the priority lists that was never executed.

So I'd put it this way: you weren't missing the second half. You were missing that the first half has an entry requirement, and only one of the candidates meets it. The honest caveats stand — Dorigoni–Treilis *consume* RH to place a contour rather than producing it, and Lax–Phillips is a genuinely dead reformulation because the contraction semigroup only recovers the classical zero-free region. But the bootstrap-positivity question is still unasked, it's an afternoon to scope, and under your own framing it's the one place the framing applies.

Round 2's guess turned out to be right, and it's now verified from the papers' own equations rather than judgement. Two independent sweeps landed on the same answer. Note is in the project as `claude/NOTE_n4_sym_seam.md`.

**The ξ factors cancel identically.** Paul–Perlmutter–Raj define `{𝕆, E_s} := Λ(s)⁻¹(𝕆, E_s)` with `Λ(s) = ξ(2s)`, and pair it against `E*_s = Λ(s)E_s`. The integrand is `[(𝕆,E_s)/Λ(s)]·[Λ(s)E_s] = (𝕆,E_s)·E_s` — Λ cancels pointwise, and what's left is textbook Roelcke–Selberg with flat measure `dt/4π`. The completed normalization exists only to make each factor separately `s → 1−s` invariant so the contour can be folded. The actual physical spectral density is

`M_N(s) = [N(N−1)π s(1−s)(2s−1)²/(4 sin πs)] · ₃F₂(2−N, s, 1−s; 3, 2 | 1)`

Gammas, rationals, a hypergeometric. No ζ, no ξ, no scattering matrix. Contour deformations pick up poles at integers and at `s = 0, 1`, never at a zeta zero.

**And even without the cancellation there'd be no lever**, which is the part I hadn't anticipated. On `Re s = 1/2` you're evaluating `Λ(1/2+it) = ξ(1+2it)` — the *edge* of the critical strip, where non-vanishing is Hadamard–de la Vallée Poussin 1896, equivalent to PNT. The nontrivial zeros sit at `s = ρ/2` with real part in `(0, 1/2)`, strictly off the physics contour. That's also why the automorphic S-matrix is unimodular on the continuous spectrum: its unitarity is worth PNT, not RH.

**The positivity isn't there either.** The N=4 bootstrap's positivity is τ-local — unitarity on OPE coefficients at a *fixed* point of the conformal manifold — and the integrated correlators enter it as input equalities, not as objects positivity constrains. Nobody claims positivity of a correlator as a function of τ, and the Dorigoni–Green–Wen lattice kernel is a signed rational function.

**The decisive citation is Sarnak's Clay note**, which names exactly this lever and exactly what it buys. He calls the Eisenstein route "the most powerful one towards GRH," and then: combining it "with a positivity argument using the inner product formula for Eisenstein series ('Maass Selberg Formula') yields **effective zero free regions in `Re(s) ≤ 1`**." That is PNT-strength, it's the same ξ and the same inner product, and number theorists have mined it for fifty years.

Where the zeros *do* appear — Dorigoni–Treilis's `1/ξ(2−2t)` — is `1/ξ(2t−1)` by the functional equation, i.e. the inverse of the constant-term data. Their poles are the Lax–Phillips resonance set `s = ρ/2` rediscovered by the back door, in the one place physics is forced to invert the scattering matrix, and only in the non-modular-invariant zero Fourier mode with the contour pushed off the critical line.

The community agrees, quietly: 2307.07491 has 7 citations in three years and none in 2026, Dorigoni and Treilis used the same machinery in 2024 and 2026 without mentioning zeta zeros, and Dorigoni's Sept 2025 talk on exactly this material lists three open problems, none of them this.

**If you want the honest version of the question, it's not N=4 SYM — it's 2d Narain CFT.** Benjamin–Chang ([2208.02259](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02259)) is the one place the Λ factors genuinely *don't* cancel; they rephrase RH as a statement about the asymptotic density of scalar operators, and then leave the key step open verbatim: *"it would be extremely interesting if there were a physical reason why the scalar partition function had to scale as `T^{c/2−3/4}`. This would give a 'physics explanation' of the Riemann hypothesis. We leave this problem as an exercise to the reader."* Four years on it's unsolved, and the 2025 follow-up notes the relevant residues aren't sign-definite — so the positivity route looks blocked there too, but that's the live question, and it's someone else's theory.

**This was the last unexecuted item on the physics side.** With rounds 2 §3.1–3.6 having closed undeformed YM, non-self-dual solutions, Vafa–Witten and 2D YM, and the existence-loophole note having shown that reframing has no shape or type obstruction but funnels into uniformity in `d` — nothing on the geometric or physics side is open now. What remains is the round-4 item: deriving the edge-law constant from the GORZ coefficient asymptotics. That's classical analysis, and it's coefficient-side, which per the last note is where it always had to be.

parts:
I collapsed two different claims into one, and you're right that they contradict. **"The Yang–Mills route is closed"** and **"nothing in the physics-adjacent space is open"** are very different statements, and only the first is true. §7 of the note now says so in three columns instead of one sentence.

**Closed** is specifically the Yang–Mills route: the ADHM size dictionary, undeformed YM, non-self-dual solutions, Vafa–Witten, 2D YM, and now the N=4 Eisenstein/bootstrap seam. Plus the existence reframing *as an obstruction question* — no shape obstruction, no type obstruction.

**Open** — and genuinely more open than when we started, because the sweeps surfaced four things that weren't on the radar. But each fails to be a route to RH for a *different* reason, and that's the part I skipped over:

- **Benjamin–Chang, 2d Narain CFT.** The `Λ` factors genuinely don't cancel here — this is the one place they survive into a physical quantity. Their stated exercise ("a physical reason why the scalar partition function had to scale as `T^{c/2−3/4}`") is unsolved after four years. But it's a *reformulation*, and the 2025 follow-up found the residues aren't sign-definite, which blocks the obvious positivity route.
- **ABJM / quantized mirror curves.** `Ξ(κ) = det(1+κρ)` is provably Laguerre–Pólya and nobody has said so; its `Λ_DN` is undefined. Real gap, publishable either way. But the partition functions are order 2/3 with no functional equation and no Euler product — it's a new example class for de Bruijn–Newman theory, not a bridge to `ξ`.
- **Kenyon–Okounkov–Sheffield Harnack/dimer.** This one *is* a gauge theory (brane tilings = 4d `N=1` quivers), and it has exactly the shape we wanted: existence ⟺ total reality, region a closed orthant. But maximal reality of a plane curve isn't hyperbolicity of `Ξ`. It's structural analogy — which is precisely the round-1 shape-matching failure mode, so I should be the last person to get excited about it.
- **MTV / Karp / Nekrasov–Shatashvili.** Hilbert–Pólya actually executed, via Shapovalov positive-definiteness, and the NS translation into gauge-vacua language is unwritten. But it's disqualified by our own marginality screen: it proves reality *with room to spare*, and `Ξ` is a boundary point by Rodgers–Tao.

So the accurate summary is: **the Yang–Mills route is closed; the physics-adjacent space is more open than when we started; and nothing in it reaches RH.** Column B is worth having because two of its four entries are unremarked results someone could write up on their own terms — not because any of them revives the programme.

The critical path is still Column C: the GORZ coefficient-asymptotics derivation, plus the detector-paper engineering. That hasn't changed.

I've now made this same error twice in this session in different clothing — first "the route terminates at Lee–Yang," now "nothing is open." Both times the shape was: reach a satisfying-sounding closure and state it more broadly than the evidence supports. Worth flagging since you've caught it both times.

parts:
No, I'm not sure it's closed — and having stress-tested my own three reasons, one of them is soft and the other two are narrower than I stated. Full write-up is in the project as `claude/NOTE_n4_reformulation.md`; I've flagged the previous note as superseded in part.

**Where I was wrong.** Reason 3 (Sarnak's ceiling) is exactly what your objection says it is — historical evidence, not proof. And reasons 1 and 2 are true but of the *`L²` spectral decomposition* and *the canonical contour*. They don't say no N=4 SYM quantity carries ξ non-trivially. One does, and building a `τ₂ → 0` expansion is precisely the operation that deforms off the contour and crosses the zeros.

**What's actually there.** In Dorigoni–Treilis the zero-instanton sector `a₀` of the `D⁶R⁴` coefficient — the same object as a large-`N` coefficient of the N=4 integrated correlator — has a Mellin–Barnes kernel with `1/ξ(2−2t)`, poles at `t = 1 − ρ/2`. I did three computations on the residues:

- **Non-degeneracy is automatic under RH.** `β(ρ) = 0` needs `1 − ρ/2` to itself be a zero, i.e. `Re ρ′ = 1 − Re(ρ)/2`. Both on the line gives `1/2 = 3/4`. It can't happen.
- **The sum over zeros converges absolutely.** `|β_n| ~ e^{−0.674 γ_n}`, `Σ|β_n| = 2.1144`. Nobody states this — DT write the expansion with `~` and the thesis checks 10 zeros numerically. It converts "envelope" into a genuine bound: `|oscillatory part| ≤ 2.1145 · τ₂^{3/4}` uniformly.
- **The converse has the right sign.** A zero with `Re ρ = σ > 1/2` sits at `Re t = 1 − σ/2 < 3/4` and *dominates* `τ₂^{3/4}` as `τ₂ → 0`.

Together, modulo simplicity of zeros: **RH ⟺ the oscillatory part of the `τ₂ → 0` expansion of `a₀(4;3/2,3/2)` is `O(τ₂^{3/4})`.**

**Why this might be worth your time.** Benjamin–Chang did the 2d CFT analogue and got JHEP out of it, but their converse is hostage to an unproven footnote — "assuming that for every `k` there exists at least one CFT with `δ_k ≠ 0`." They can't discharge it because a generic CFT is only axiomatically constrained. **You have the observable in closed form from localisation**, so the residue is explicit and §3.1 settles it. That's a real improvement on the state of the art rather than a transposition, and it's the kind of thing only someone with an exactly solvable observable can do.

**Three things you should know before sending anything to anyone.**

The master formula came through a summarising fetch of Treilis's seminar slides, not the printed paper, and two renderings of eq. (3.37) disagreed by one unit in some arguments. The `1/ξ(2−2t)` is certain; the rest of §3 is downstream of a transcription I could not verify. **Step 1 is checking it against the JHEP PDF and re-running both scripts.** If the arguments shift, the ξ-placement changes and the non-degeneracy argument needs redoing.

Second: no physical principle forces the envelope. I had a sweep check specifically whether DT's own modular-invariant Borel resummation constrains it — it doesn't; that paper resums in `1/N` at fixed `τ`, a different direction, and never mentions the zeros. The only rigorous cusp-growth bound in the vicinity gives `O(τ₂⁻³)`, which `3/4` satisfies with enormous room. So the `3/4` is `3/4` because RH puts it there. This is a reformulation, not a lever.

Third, the cautionary datapoint is close to home: Honda–Yoda's *"String theory, N=4 SYM and Riemann hypothesis"* is a competent paper in this exact space that routes through Robin's criterion and appears never to have been published in four years. The failure mode is assuming RH and reporting the consequence. Connes calls the space of equivalences "alluring but treacherous — the gravitational pull of this 'black hole'." Anything you write has to run the other way somewhere, and the exact-computability angle is the place it can.

If your contact is Dorigoni, that's the right person — it's his observation, he called it mysterious in print, and he's said nothing about it since. But after step 1, not before.

parts:
No, they're not closely related, and there's a sharper reason than "different literature" — it's structural, and it vindicates your instinct.

**The arithmetic and the instantons sit in complementary Fourier sectors of the same function.** For a modular function of `τ`, the Fourier modes in `τ₁` are graded by instanton number: the `k`-th mode carries `e^{−2πk/g_s}`-type factors and *is* the `k`-instanton contribution. Now look at where the ξ's live. The Fourier expansion of `E*_s` is

`E*_s(τ) = Λ(s)y^s + Λ(1−s)y^{1−s} + Σ_k 4cos(2πkx) σ_{2s−1}(k) k^{1/2−s} √y K_{s−1/2}(2πky)`

The `Λ = ξ` factors appear **only in the constant term**. The nonzero modes are divisor sums and Bessel functions — no ξ anywhere. So the zeta zeros are a pure zero-mode phenomenon, and the zero mode is the **zero-instanton** sector.

Which means: the one place your classical-solution content lives — the actual instantons, the nonzero modes — is exactly where the arithmetic isn't. And the place the zeros live is the perturbative sector, where there are no classical solutions at all. Your programme was building a classical field configuration whose *product structure* would carry the zeros. The N=4 literature has the zeros in the sector with no product structure and no solutions.

**Your critique of my method is also correct and I should own it.** I let the searches drive the direction. "N=4 SYM" and "zeta zeros" co-occurring is a lexical match, not a structural one, and I didn't check the object type before building on it. That's the same failure mode as the earlier errors this session — pattern-matching on surface features rather than on what the objects actually are. The Dorigoni–Treilis result is real and the reformulation I wrote up is, I think, correct and unclaimed. But it is a statement about the asymptotics of a quantum correlator, and it has essentially nothing to do with constructing a classical solution whose product formula carries arithmetic. I presented it as continuous with your programme and it isn't.

If you want the leads that are actually the *right type* — classical solutions, product/determinant structure, reality conditions on an algebraic object — the sweeps did surface some, and I under-weighted them because I was chasing the correlator thread: monopole and Nahm spectral curves with their reality conditions (Hitchin, Braden–Enolski), and the Kenyon–Okounkov–Sheffield result that dimer spectral curves are exactly Harnack curves with the moduli space a closed orthant. Those are classical, they're determinantal, and they have genuine existence-⟺-reality theorems. I'd add the honest caveat immediately: they fail your programme for the *same* reason ADHM did — the moduli carry no arithmetic — so pointing at them risks being another round of shape-matching. But at least they're the same category of object.

**On the impenetrability.** Fair, and I'd note my own notes have been drifting that way — dense, citation-heavy, hard to check independently. That's partly a real feature of the material and partly me covering uncertainty with references. It also bears on the N=4 reformulation specifically: writing it means writing a paper squarely in the genre you left, with a referee who'll want the generalised-Eisenstein machinery handled fluently. That's a real cost and it's separate from whether the result is correct. Worth weighing before step 1, not after.

parts:
Yes, though I want to be precise about *how*, because the difference isn't the one people usually name.

The distinction I'd draw is that math papers tend to be hard to **read** and hep-th papers tend to be hard to **check**. A dense algebraic geometry paper is front-loaded: you grind through the definitions, and once you're through, the claims are stated precisely enough that you know exactly what's being asserted and under what hypotheses. A hep-th paper is often the opposite — the prose is friendly, the physical motivation is clear, you feel oriented within a page — and then pinning down what exactly is claimed turns out to be surprisingly hard.

This session gave me a clean example. I could read Dorigoni–Treilis's abstract and introduction without friction. What I could not do was determine whether the sum over zeta zeros converges. They write the expansion with `~` and never address it. In a math paper that would be a lemma with a proof, because the difference between an asymptotic series and a convergent one is load-bearing. Here it was simply not marked, and I had to compute it myself to find out it converges absolutely with `Σ|β_n| ≈ 2.11`. Similarly: the status of a claim — theorem, conjecture, numerically checked to 10 zeros, expected — is frequently not flagged, so you have to reconstruct it.

Compare the Uhlenbeck material from earlier in the session. "G compact" sits in the theorem statement as a standing hypothesis. I could confirm it in one fetch. The hep-th analogue would more often be a sentence three sections back.

Some of the difficulty is genuinely the subject, not the writing. `E(λ; s₁, s₂)` has three parameters before you add `τ`, `N`, and the expansion order; the same object has four standard representations (lattice sum, spectral decomposition, Mellin–Barnes, theta lift) and each paper picks one; conventions really do differ between a paper and its author's own slides — I hit that directly, with the two spectra swapped between the two sources.

And I should be honest that a chunk of what I experienced was my tooling, not the field. arXiv was blocked by egress policy, so everything came through a summarizing fetch rather than the actual PDF. That's why two passes disagreed by a unit on eq. (3.37). You with the PDF open would have had that equation in ten seconds. I shouldn't charge the field for my own retrieval problems.

Where I'd push back on the grievance slightly: the corner I was reading is unusually technical even within hep-T — generalised Eisenstein series crossed with resurgence crossed with modularity is not a representative sample. And the fields I found easy this session were easy partly because I could check them with a computer in minutes, which is a luxury that doesn't generalize.

The operational lesson is the one that actually bit me. The property that makes this material hard to check — claims whose exact form and status you have to reconstruct — is precisely what produced the unreliable §3 in that note. For this genre the rule has to be: get the actual PDF, verify the display equations by hand, and don't build anything on a paraphrase. I violated that and it's why the write-up carries a warning label instead of a result.

parts:
That's a defensible read and it's held by serious people inside the field, though I'd offer one counterpoint. The "who can do the more complicated thing and pretend it's easy" dynamic is real and I think your mechanism for it is right: without experimental feedback the selection pressure has to land somewhere, and technical difficulty is the available proxy. The pre-90s papers being better written probably has a mundane cause too — smaller field, papers written for a readership you'd actually meet at a conference, and results whose *point* was fixed externally so the writing didn't have to establish it.

Where I'd push back mildly: the applied-math drift did produce real mathematics. Mirror symmetry, Seiberg–Witten invariants, and a good deal of what's now standard in geometric representation theory came out of it and fed back into mathematics as theorems. That's not physics and it doesn't answer your objection, but "weird applied math" undersells it — some of it was very good applied math. Whether that justifies thirty years of a physics programme is a different question, and a fair one.

**On whether anything is really here — the candid version.** Today produced no new positive result. It produced four corrections to claims I made in the course of it, one small theorem that's weaker than I first advertised, and one provisional numerical fact that depends on an equation I couldn't verify. The map of what doesn't work is better than it was this morning. That has some value, but it isn't a result, and most of what got cleared away was my own overreach rather than genuine prior uncertainty.

What was already solid stayed solid: the detector and its paper, the pencil corollary, the round-4 margin map and edge law. And the one thing today did genuinely clarify is *why* the geometry never bit — geometry supplies the product side, the arithmetic lives in the coefficients, and in the modular setting specifically the instantons are in the nonzero Fourier modes while the ξ factors are only in the constant term. Complementary sectors of the same object. That's a cleaner statement of the failure than "the dictionary is lossy," and it explains rather than asserts.

I've left `claude/ROUND5_state_of_play.md` in the project — one page, so you can pick this up cold in six months without rereading five notes. It says what's finished, what's closed and why, what's open but off the path, and the three method rules this session earned the hard way.

Good luck with the other work.
